Read in the data:
```{r}
candy_file <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/candy-power-ranking/candy-data.csv"

candy = read.csv(candy_file, row.names=1)
head(candy)
```

> Q1. How many different candy types are in this dataset?

```{r}
nrow(candy)
```

> Q2. How many fruity candy types are in the dataset?

```{r}
sum(candy$fruity)
```

Analyzing `winpercent`:

```{r}
candy["Twix", ]$winpercent
```

```{r}
library(dplyr)

candy |> 
  filter(row.names(candy)=="Twix") |> 
  select(winpercent)
```
> Q3. What is your favorite candy (other than Twix) in the dataset and what is it’s `winpercent` value?

```{r}
candy["Almond Joy", ]$winpercent
```


> Q4. What is the `winpercent` value for “Kit Kat”?

```{r}
candy["Kit Kat", ]$winpercent
```

> Q5. What is the `winpercent` value for “Tootsie Roll Snack Bars”?

```{r}
candy["Tootsie Roll Snack Bars", ]$winpercent
```

Using `skim()` from the `skimr` package:
```{r}
library("skimr")
skim(candy)
```

> Q6. Is there any variable/column that looks to be on a different scale to the majority of the other columns in the dataset?

Yes, it looks like the last three columns are all representing percentages, differing from the other 9 that are all binary (1/0). The `winpercent` column in particular is written in % form rather than decimal form (i.e., 50 instead of 0.50), so it has much larger values than any other column. 

> Q7. What do you think a zero and one represent for the candy$chocolate column?

The 0 represents that there are zero observations missing. The 1 represents that all observations are present/observations are present for 100% of rows.

## Exploratory Analysis

> Q8. Plot a histogram of winpercent values using both base R and ggplot2.

Base R:
```{r}
hist(candy$winpercent)
```
ggplot:
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(candy, aes(x = winpercent)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15)
```

> Q9. Is the distribution of winpercent values symmetrical?

The center of the distribution is slightly shifted to the left to around 40%. As a result, the distribution is somewhat asymmetrical with bias towards lower values.

> Q10. Is the center of the distribution above or below 50%?

The center is *below* 50%. 

> Q11. On average is chocolate candy higher or lower ranked than fruit candy?

```{r}
chocolatepercent <- candy$winpercent[as.logical(candy$chocolate)]
fruitypercent <- candy$winpercent[as.logical(candy$fruity)]
meanchoc <- mean(chocolatepercent)
meanfru <- mean(fruitypercent)
meanchoc
meanfru
```

Chocolate candy is, on average, **higher** ranked than fruit candy.

> Q12. Is this difference statistically significant?

```{r}
t.test(x = chocolatepercent, y = fruitypercent)
```
The different *is* statistically significant.

## Overall Candy Rankings

> Q13. What are the five least liked candy types in this set?

```{r}
library(dplyr)
leastliked <- candy %>% arrange(winpercent)
head(leastliked)
```
The five *least* liked candy types in this set are Nik L Nip, Boston Baked Beans, Chiclets, Super Bubble, and Jawbusters.

> Q14. What are the top 5 all time favorite candy types out of this set?

```{r}
mostliked <- candy %>% arrange(desc(winpercent))
head(mostliked)
```
The five *most* liked candy types in this set are Reese's Peanut Butter cup, Reese's Miniatures, Twix, Kit Kat, and Snickers.

> Q15. Make a first barplot of candy ranking based on winpercent values.

```{r}
ggplot(candy, aes(winpercent, rownames(candy))) +
  geom_col()
```

> Q16. This is quite ugly, use the reorder() function to get the bars sorted by winpercent?

```{r}
ggplot(candy, aes(winpercent, reorder(rownames(candy), winpercent))) +
  geom_col()
```

Add some color:

```{r}
my_cols=rep("black", 85)
my_cols[as.logical(candy$chocolate)] = "chocolate"
my_cols[as.logical(candy$bar)] = "brown"
my_cols[as.logical(candy$fruity)] = "lightpink"

ggplot(candy) + 
  aes(winpercent, reorder(rownames(candy),winpercent)) +
  geom_col(fill=my_cols) +
  ylab("")
```

> Q17. What is the worst ranked chocolate candy?

The worst ranked chocolate candy is Sixlets.

> Q18. What is the best ranked fruity candy?

The best ranked fruity candy is Starburst.



## Analyzing `pricepercent`

```{r}
library(ggrepel)

my_cols[as.logical(candy$fruity)] = "red"

ggplot(candy) + 
  aes(x = winpercent, y = pricepercent, label = rownames(candy)) +
  geom_point(col = my_cols) +
  geom_text_repel(col = my_cols, size = 3.3, max.overlaps = 5)
```

> Q19. Which candy type is the highest ranked in terms of winpercent for the least money - i.e. offers the most bang for your buck?

Based on the figure, Reese's Miniatures is the highest ranked candy below `pricepercent = 50`. It has a win rate over 80% with a price point of only 0.279 (27.9%). 

> Q20. What are the top 5 most expensive candy types in the dataset and of these which is the least popular?

```{r}
expensive <- candy %>% arrange(desc(pricepercent))
head(expensive)
```
The top 5 most expensive candy types are Nik L Nip, Nestle Smarties, Ring Pop, Hershey's Krackel, and Hershey's Milk Chocolate.
Of these, Nik L Nip is the least popular. 

## Correlation Structure

```{r}
library(corrplot)
cij <- cor(candy)
corrplot(cij)
```

> Q22. Examining this plot what two variables are anti-correlated (i.e. have minus values)?

Chocolate and fruity are the most strongly anti-correlated pair. 

Other, less-strongly anti-correlated pairs include:

- Fruity & bar
- Pluribus & bar
- Pricepercent & fruity
- Peanutyalmondy & fruity
- Winpercent & fruity
- Etc.

> Q23. Use your corrplot result to make a prediction: which variables do you expect will have the largest contributions (i.e. loadings) to PC1 (i.e., drive the most separation between candies along the first principal component)?

I expect that chocolate and fruity will drive the most separation in PC1, because they are the most strongly anti-correlated. This will drive separation of the data into distinct clusters. 

## Principal Component Analysis

```{r}
pca <- prcomp(candy, scale = TRUE)
summary(pca)
```

```{r}
ggplot(pca$x) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2) +
  geom_point(col = my_cols)
```

```{r}
my_data <- cbind(candy, pca$x)
p <- ggplot(my_data) + 
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, size = winpercent/100, text = rownames(my_data), label = rownames(my_data)) +
  geom_point(col = my_cols)
p
```


> Q24. Complete the code to generate the “Halloween Candy PCA Space Map” above. Be sure to have legible labels along with a plot title and subtitle:

```{r}
p + geom_text_repel(size=3.3, col=my_cols, max.overlaps = 7)  + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(label = rownames(candy),
       title = "Halloween Candy PCA Space",
       subtitle = "Colored by type: chocolate bar (dark brown), chocolate other(light brown), fruity (red), other (black)")
```

> Q25. Complete the code to generate the loadings plot above. What original variables are picked up strongly by PC1 in the positive direction? Do these make sense to you? Where did you see this relationship highlighted previously?

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(PC1, reorder(colnames(candy), PC1)) +
  geom_col()
```

The variables picked up strongly in the positive direction were `fruity`, `pluribus`, and `hard`. In the correlation plot, `pluribus` and `hard` were the only two variables that `fruity` was positively correlated with, so it makes sense that they would be grouped together. It also makes sense with general knowledge/intuitively-- fruit candy is more likely to have these two traits than others like `caramel` or `nougat`.

> Q26. Based on your exploratory analysis, correlation findings, and PCA results, what combination of characteristics appears to make a “winning” candy? How do these different analyses (visualization, correlation, PCA) support or complement each other in reaching this conclusion?

In the plot of `winpercent`, we can see that chocolate candy tends to be on top of the graph/have higher popularity than non-chocolate candy. In the correlation plot, we can see that `chocolate` and `fruity` are strongly anticorrelated, and that they seem to each be positively correlated with a *separate* set of variables. Therefore, we can expect to see two distinct groups/clusters in our PCA analysis. Then, looking at our PCA plot, we can in fact see a clear separation of chocolate and fruit candy. In addition, the chocolate candy seems to have separated into two groups as well-- bar and non-bar. In the loadings plot, we can then see which side of the plot `winpercent` is associated with, and other variables that are associated with the same side. `winpercent` strongly influences points towards the negative/left side of the plot. More negative numbers are also strongly associated with `chocolate` and `bar`. This indicates that a "winning" candy tends to be a type of chocolate bar. 


## PCA from Scratch 

Read in the mystery dataset:
```{r}
m <- read.csv("mystery.csv")
head(m)
```

Visualize with a 3D scatterplot:
```{r}
library(scatterplot3d)
scatterplot3d(m)
```

> Q27. Hmm… can you tell what the mystery dataset represents from this 3D plot? Hint: It is something that goes well with chocolate in Barry’s opnion.

It doesn't really seem possible to tell just from the plot. It's not clear to me yet what this data represents.

Compute the covariance matrix:
```{r}
cij <- cov(m)
cij
```

Eigen decomposition of covariance matrix:
```{r}
ans <- eigen(cij)
eigenval <- ans$values   # variance captured by each PC
eigenvec <- ans$vectors  # the new axes (principal components)
```

How much variance does each PC capture?
```{r}
round(cumsum(eigenval) / sum(eigenval) * 100, 2)
```

> Q28. What percentage of the total variance is captured by the first two principal components together? Does this seem like enough to get a meaningful 2D representation of a 3D object?

Together, the first two PCs capture 83.49% of the variance. This seems like a reasonably sufficient amount to get a meaningful 2D visualization.

Now, set up & create the 2D plot:
```{r}
# Step 3: Project data onto the top 2 eigenvectors
scores <- as.matrix(m) %*% eigenvec[, 1:2]

# Set some colnames for easier plotting
colnames(scores) <- c("PC1", "PC2")

ggplot(scores) +
  aes(PC1, PC2) +
  geom_point()
```

> Q29. What is the mystery dataset? Does it make sense that PCA was able to recover a recognizable 2D view from 3D data? What has been “lost” in the reduction from 3D to 2D?

It maybe looks like some kind of cup-- maybe a cup of tea? It does make sense that PCA was able to recover something recognizable. In the reduction, it lost the 3-dimensionality that was making the visualization hard to understand. You do lose some information about the data, but you can better understand what's left.

Verify with `prcomp()`:

```{r}
p <- prcomp(m)
summary(p)

ggplot(p$x) +
  aes(PC1, PC2) +
  geom_point(size=2, col="steelblue", alpha=0.5) +
  labs(title="Mystery dataset: PCA projection",
       subtitle="3D structure recovered in 2D") +
  theme_bw()
```

> Q30. Do the results from prcomp() match your manual eigen decomposition? The scores may differ in sign (direction) — this is normal and does not affect interpretation. Why do you think this is?

It looks like the manual version plotted the data upside-down-- now, in the correct direction, it is clear that the data is representing a teapot. However, even though the plot from before had a different sign, it still matches the same shape as in the `prcomp()` version. Maybe this could be because it's random whether a particular set of traits is assigned to one end of the PC axis or another. I.e., negative and positive could be swapped and the same variation would still be represented.
